title: The Exponential Decay Law
short: N = N₀e^(−λt), the activity is A = λN, and the half-life is ln 2/λ.
trouble: Students mix up the decay constant with the half-life, or the activity with the number of nuclei.

blocks.html: In Chemistry you used half-lives: after each one, half of the remaining nuclei are left. Calculus shows why the pattern is exponential, and it adds two useful quantities: the decay constant and the activity. The key fact is that a nucleus has no memory: an old uranium nucleus is exactly as likely to decay in the next second as a new one.

Each nucleus decays with the same probability $\lambda\,dt$ in a short time $dt$, so $$\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N(t) = N_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$ The half-life is $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$, the mean life is $\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}$, and the activity (decays per second, in becquerels, Bq) is $$A = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$

With $N$ nuclei, each decaying with probability $\lambda\,dt$, the expected number of decays in $dt$ is $\lambda N\,dt$, so $dN = -\lambda N\,dt$. Separate the variables: $\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt$, so $\ln N = -\lambda t + C$ and $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, the exponential whose derivative is proportional to itself. The half-life comes from $\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$: take logs, $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$. A big $\lambda$ means a short half-life: they are inverses, not the same thing. And the activity is the decay rate, $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$: a sample with many nuclei but a long half-life can have a small activity.

blocks.name: ph-nucleus
blocks.cap: 400 nuclei, each with a 2-second half-life, decaying at random. No one can say which nucleus goes next, yet the count follows $N_0e^{-\lambda t}$ closely: about half are left after each half-life.

blocks.title: Carbon-14's decay constant
blocks.q: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. Find its decay constant per year and per second.

blocks.title: The activity of a gram of radium
blocks.q: Radium-226 has a half-life of 1600 years and a molar mass of 226 g/mol. What is the activity of 1.00 g of it?
blocks.a: $3.7 \times 10^{10}$ decays per second, which is how the old unit, the curie, was defined

blocks.title: How much is left?
blocks.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.02 days. What fraction of a sample remains after 30.0 days?

blocks.html: Each nucleus decays on its own, at random. So the number of decays counted in a short time jumps around a little from one count to the next, scattered about the average $\lambda N\,\Delta t$. With the enormous numbers of nuclei in any real sample, the smooth exponential describes it extremely well, as the simulation above shows even for 400 nuclei.

Mixing up the decay constant with the half-life, or the activity with the number of nuclei. $\lambda$ has units of 1/time and is large when the half-life is short: $\lambda = \ln 2/T_{1/2}$. The activity counts decays per second ($A = \lambda N$), not nuclei. Check the units: $A$ in Bq (per second) needs $\lambda$ in s⁻¹, so convert years to seconds first.
